what_it_does: When a large language model generates text one word at a time, each step requires reading a large 'KV cache' — a scratchpad storing the key and value vectors computed for every previous word — from memory. This read-heavy operation moves far more data than the math it feeds, so the GPU's computation units sit idle waiting for memory; in other words, the bottleneck is memory bandwidth, not raw compute power. PAISE (PIM-Accelerated Inference Scheduling Engine) attacks this by offloading the attention computation — the step that reads the KV cache and computes relevance scores — from the GPU to specially augmented memory chips called HBM-PIM (High-Bandwidth Memory with Processing-In-Memory), where small arithmetic units live physically inside the memory stack and can process data without sending it over the wire to the GPU. A scheduling algorithm decides, for each layer and attention head of the model, whether it runs faster on the GPU or in the PIM memory, based on each device's bandwidth and compute capacity. A custom software kernel restructures how data from multiple attention heads is read across the PIM chip's internal banks to squeeze out maximum parallelism.
